Yibo Wen1,Han Liu 1
on behalf of the Autonomous Science Bench Team
1Northwestern University
Abstract.AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a
limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active
experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduceAutonomous Science Bench, an initial release
comprising six budgeted design–build–test–learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology,
chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service,
and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires
passing two calibrated gates: adiscoverygate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and alearning
gate, which evaluates its model’s ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent–model
configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is
solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate
rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen
designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1
of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard athttps://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.
Correspondence:hanliu@northwestern.edu

4 Results
This section examines how well agents perform and at what cost (Section 4.1), which gate they miss when
they fail (Section 4.2), and how they spend their budget across rounds (Section 4.3). App. B lists the
outcome and both gate scores of every trial.
4.1 Cost and Agent Performance
Overall success is limited.Only 31 of the 144 trials pass. Opus 5.5 in Claude Code resolves 67% of cam-
paign trials, and GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-5.6 Luna in Codex follow at 44% and 28% (Figure 3a). Sonnet 5.5
and GLM-5.3 Flash resolve two trials each, Qwen3.8 27B and MiniMax M3 one each, and Haiku 4.5 none.
Even Opus 5.5 resolves every trial on only two campaigns and fails all three biosensor trials. App. B gives
every configuration’s results by campaign.
Every campaign separates configurations.Each campaign is resolved by some configurations and missed by
others. The oxygen-evolution campaign is resolved most often, in 8 of 24 trials by four configurations, and the
coercivity campaign least, in 3 of 24, two of them by Opus 5.5. Only the two GPT-5.6 configurations resolve
the biosensor campaign. Resolution counts are similar across domains in this sample, at 9, 11, and 11 of 48
trials in bio

6 Limitations
Scale.Version 0.1 contains six campaigns in three fields and evaluates eight agent–model configurations, a small
sample of both experimental science and agents. We plan to add campaigns, fields, and configurations, and a
source registry and contribution guide let research groups contribute campaigns from their own experiments.
Replays and twins.A replay backend returns only previously recorded measurements, while a twin’s reliability
depends on its surrogate’s training coverage. Both limit the design space available to agents.
Public data.The campaigns use published experiments that a model may have memorized or an agent could
retrieve during a trial if egress controls fail to fully block access. Fully addressing them requires unpublished
results from live experiments or autonomous laboratories, which the planned live backend is designed to support.
7 Conclusion
Science advances through decisions about which experiments are worth a limited budget. Autonomous Science
Bench evaluates these choices in campaigns grounded in published lab data, measuring what agents discover and
what they learn separately. Our results show why both matter. Agents can find strong designs without learning
to rank unseen ones, or learn useful rankings without reaching the best designs. Even the strongest evaluated
agent remains unreliable across campaigns, and an overall success rate alone obscures these distinct weaknesses.
We release the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard as a first step toward evaluation that progress
from replayed experiments through digital twins to autonomous laboratories. As this evaluation moves into
live science, agents will face broader decisions about which questions to pursue and which experiments to run.
The proposed scheduler would allocate scarce measurements to help identify which agents to trust with these
decisions. Together, these steps offer a path toward autonomous science in which agents turn limited experimental
resources into reliable discoveries and new questions worth pursuing.
